error_modes.label: ANTI-G SUIT SERVICEABILITY AND OPERATION CHECK

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete anti-G suit check during the pre-flight and the pre-maneuver flow, did not verify hose connection, valve function and suit fit before entering the portion of the profile requiring more than 3Gs. SP did not detect that the suit failed to inflate on the first application above 3G and continued the maneuver sequence with no serviceability call. The IP had to direct a knock-it-off and assume control to unload the aircraft, and the resulting excursion exceeded 300 feet from the assigned altitude and 20 knots from the target airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a hurried anti-G suit check that stopped at the visual connection and omitted the inflation verification, entered the high-G portion of the profile without confirming proper suit operation. SP recognized the absence of suit inflation only after the IP prompted verbally and delayed the decision to unload, so the deviation reached 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed before the aircraft was recovered to the assigned parameters. No physical intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an anti-G suit check performed out of the normal sequence, entered the first maneuver above 3G before completing the inflation verification. SP recognized the omission on the initial G application, unloaded promptly, completed the check and re-entered the maneuver without any prompting or intervention from the IP. The excursion during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP checked the anti-G suit connection, valve operation and fit before flight and verified proper inflation on the first application above 3G. SP called the suit serviceable, adjusted the fit as required and continued the profile with altitude held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots. The suit check was completed without interruption to the planned maneuver sequence.
texts.4: SP verified anti-G suit connection, valve function and fit before flight, confirmed inflation at the first G onset and rechecked operation after each maneuver set. SP integrated the check into the maneuver flow so smoothly that no attention was diverted from aircraft control, with altitude and airspeed deviations remaining negligible throughout the high-G portion of the profile.
texts.marginal: SP completed the anti-G suit check and confirmed inflation, but the check was consistently performed late, immediately before the first G application rather than during the pre-maneuver flow. The suit was serviceable and parameters remained within standards, yet the trend was toward compressing the check into the entry to the maneuver. SP is expected to move the suit verification earlier in the flow so that serviceability is established well before the first application above 3G.

error_modes.label: AGSM EXECUTION TECHNIQUE PER TECHNIQUES AND PROCEDURES MANUAL

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect breathing and straining technique, did not perform the AGSM in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual: the leg, abdominal and chest muscle tension was not sustained and the breathing cycle was longer than the prescribed interval. SP showed loss of peripheral vision and delayed response to IP calls during sustained loading above 3G. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft, and the recovery produced deviations beyond 300 feet in altitude and beyond 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an inconsistent strain and breathing cycle, performed an AGSM that did not match the technique prescribed in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with muscle tension relaxing between breathing cycles. SP restored the correct cycle only after the IP called it verbally and the correction was delayed by several seconds of sustained loading. Altitude reached the 300 foot limit and the exit heading reached 10 degrees off target before parameters were re-established, without intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially long breathing cycle, applied an AGSM that did not fully match the prescribed technique at the entry to the maneuver. SP recognized the onset of visual symptoms, tightened the muscle tension and shortened the breathing cycle to the prescribed interval without any prompting or intervention. Altitude and exit heading deviations during the correction remained between 150 and 300 feet and between 5 and 10 degrees.
texts.3: SP performed the AGSM in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with sustained leg, abdominal and chest muscle tension and the prescribed breathing cycle maintained throughout the loading. SP showed no degradation of vision or response, kept the scan running through the maneuver and held altitude within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP executed the AGSM exactly as prescribed in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with correctly timed strain and breathing cycles and tension adjusted to the actual G level rather than applied uniformly. SP sustained the maneuver without any degradation of vision, voice or aircraft control, and deviations in altitude, airspeed and exit heading were negligible for the whole high-G portion of the profile.
texts.marginal: SP performed the AGSM to the prescribed technique and remained within standards, but the strain effort was applied at a level higher than required for the G actually being pulled, which produced early fatigue toward the end of the maneuver set. The technique itself was correct and no symptoms appeared, yet the trend was toward loss of effectiveness on the later repetitions. SP is expected to modulate the strain effort to the G level so that the AGSM remains effective through the whole sequence.

error_modes.label: AGSM ANTICIPATION AND TIMING RELATIVE TO G ONSET

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management in the entry to the maneuver, left the AGSM until after the G had already built past 3G and treated the strain as a reaction rather than as a planned action. SP was still setting power and clearing the area when the loading arrived, so the straining maneuver started late and was never fully established. The IP had to intervene on the controls to unload the aircraft, and the exit was flown more than 300 feet from the assigned altitude and more than 20 knots off the target airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to task saturation during the maneuver entry, began the AGSM after G onset instead of anticipating it as required by the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP established the correct strain only after the IP prompted verbally, and by then the delay had allowed the altitude to reach the 300 foot limit and the airspeed to reach 20 knots from target. Parameters were re-established without any intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a compressed task sequence at the entry, started the AGSM slightly after the initial G onset rather than immediately before it. SP recognized the late start on the first repetition, re-sequenced the pre-entry tasks and anticipated the strain correctly on the following maneuvers with no prompting from the IP. Deviations during the first repetition stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP anticipated each G application, completed the pre-entry tasks early and established the AGSM immediately before the loading built above 3G. SP maintained the strain through the whole loaded portion and released it in a controlled manner on unloading, holding altitude within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP sequenced clearing, power and configuration tasks so that the cockpit was quiet before every G application and the AGSM was established ahead of the onset on each repetition without exception. SP adjusted the timing to the different onset rates of the maneuvers flown and kept the aircraft on parameters with negligible deviations throughout.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated the AGSM and remained within standards, but the margin between the start of the strain and the G onset was small and shrank as the sortie progressed and workload increased. Timing was still adequate on every repetition and no symptoms appeared, yet the trend was toward reacting to the loading rather than preceding it. SP is expected to protect the pre-entry sequence so that the strain is consistently established before the onset regardless of workload.

texts.0: SP, due to overconfidence in the margin available at that airspeed and bank, applied an abrupt aft stick input without reference to the G indication and exceeded the aircraft G-limit for the configuration flown. SP did not call the exceedance and continued the profile as briefed. The IP took the controls, terminated the maneuver sequence and directed a return to base, and the recovery was flown more than 300 feet from the assigned altitude and more than 20 knots from the target airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an overconfident assessment of the recovery margin, allowed the G to build to the aircraft limit for the configuration during the pull and did not monitor the G indication during the application. SP relaxed the back pressure only after the IP called the G value, and the delayed correction left the altitude at the 300 foot limit and the airspeed at 20 knots from target. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rapid initial stick input, allowed the G to build faster than planned and approached but did not reach the aircraft limit for the configuration. SP detected the trend on the G indication, eased the back pressure and re-established the briefed loading without any prompting or intervention from the IP. Altitude deviation during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet and airspeed between 10 and 20 knots.
texts.3: SP applied smooth and progressive control inputs, monitored the G indication through each application and kept the loading within the aircraft G-limits for the configuration flown. SP matched the G applied to the maneuver briefed rather than to the maximum available, and held altitude within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP controlled the onset rate as well as the peak value, kept every application comfortably inside the aircraft G-limits for the configuration and adjusted the loading to the entry airspeed on each repetition. SP verbalized the G being flown against the limit for the configuration and maintained parameters with negligible deviations throughout the profile.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the aircraft G-limits on every application, but the peak values were consistently close to the limit for the configuration and the onset rate was faster than the maneuver required. No exceedance occurred and parameters stayed within standards, yet the trend was toward using the whole available margin on routine repetitions. SP is expected to fly the G value briefed for the maneuver and to reserve the upper part of the envelope for cases that actually require it.

error_modes.label: AWARENESS OF G LOADING AND RECOGNITION OF SYMPTOMS

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of awareness of the significance of the available G indication and of the first physiological cues, did not maintain awareness of G loading during the maneuvers and did not report the onset of greyout to the IP. SP continued the sequence with a degraded scan and did not respond to two consecutive IP calls. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and terminate the maneuver, and the excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that excluded the G indication during the loaded portion of the maneuvers, lost awareness of the actual G being pulled and of the accumulated exposure across the sequence. SP reported the loss of peripheral vision only after the IP asked directly, and the unloading was delayed, leaving the altitude at the 300 foot limit and the exit heading 10 degrees off target. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the outside reference during the pull, included the G indication in the scan later than required on the first repetitions. SP recognized the first symptoms of reduced peripheral vision, unloaded the aircraft immediately, reported the condition to the IP and re-entered the sequence with the G indication in the scan. Deviations stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 5 and 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.3: SP maintained awareness of G loading during all maneuvers, kept the G indication in the scan and knew at all times the value being pulled and the cumulative exposure of the sequence. SP reported physiological status to the IP when asked without hesitation and held altitude within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP maintained continuous awareness of G loading, anticipated the exposure of each planned maneuver, tracked the cumulative effect over the sequence and adjusted the AGSM and the pacing of the repetitions accordingly. SP reported physiological status without prompting, kept the scan complete under load and produced negligible deviations in altitude, airspeed and exit heading.
texts.marginal: SP maintained awareness of G loading and reported status accurately, but the awareness was reconstructed after each maneuver rather than tracked during it, and the G indication entered the scan only at the exit. Parameters remained within standards and no symptoms went unreported, yet the trend was toward retrospective rather than continuous awareness. SP is expected to keep the G value in the running cross-check during the loaded portion of every maneuver.

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that collapsed onto the outside reference during the strain, did not maintain the assigned altitude while manoeuvring above 3G and did not detect the developing vertical trend. The altitude deviation exceeded 300 feet and continued to increase, and SP did not initiate a correction. The IP intervened on the controls to return the aircraft to the assigned altitude and terminate the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check interrupted by the AGSM, did not maintain the assigned altitude during the loaded portion of the maneuvers and allowed the deviation to reach 300 feet. SP started the correction only after the IP called the altitude verbally, and the recovery was slow with the aircraft settling back on altitude several seconds later. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed return of the altimeter to the scan after each G application, allowed the altitude to deviate between 150 and 300 feet from the assigned value during the maneuvers. SP detected the deviation on the exit of the first repetition and corrected it promptly and smoothly, with no prompting or intervention from the IP, and subsequent repetitions were flown closer to the assigned altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the maneuvers requiring more than 3Gs, keeping the altimeter in the cross-check during the loaded portion and correcting small trends before they developed. Corrections were smooth, timely and made without prompting.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitude with deviations that were negligible in both the entry and the exit of every high-G maneuver, anticipating the vertical trend from the pitch attitude rather than reacting to the altimeter. The aircraft was flown back onto the reference altitude with corrections small enough to be barely perceptible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the assigned altitude within standards, but the deviations were consistently in the same direction on every repetition and the correction was always applied at the exit rather than during the maneuver. The values stayed inside the required tolerance, yet the trend was toward a repeated one-sided error. SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the cross-check through the loaded portion so that the deviation is trapped as it develops.

texts.0: SP, due to power and back pressure applied without reference to the airspeed indication during the strain, did not maintain the target airspeed for the maneuvers above 3G. The airspeed deviated by more than 20 knots and continued to diverge without any corrective input from SP, which reduced the margin available for the planned G. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and re-establish the target airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed power setting held through the loaded portion regardless of the energy state, allowed the airspeed to deviate to the 20 knot limit during the maneuvers. SP adjusted power only after the IP called the airspeed, and the correction was late enough that the following entry was flown from an incorrect energy state. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power adjustment at the entry to the maneuver, allowed the airspeed to deviate between 10 and 20 knots from the target value under load. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indication, corrected power promptly and re-established the target airspeed before the exit without prompting or intervention from the IP.
texts.3: SP maintained the target airspeed within 10 knots throughout the maneuvers requiring more than 3Gs, matching power to the G being applied and keeping the airspeed indication in the cross-check during the loaded portion. Corrections were small, timely and made without prompting.
texts.4: SP controlled airspeed with negligible deviations across the whole high-G sequence, anticipating the energy loss of each application and setting power before the deviation appeared. Every maneuver was entered from the correct energy state and exited on the target airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the target airspeed within standards, but the deviations were repeatedly on the low side and the power correction was applied only after the airspeed had already started to decay. The values stayed inside the required tolerance, yet the trend was toward a shrinking energy margin over the maneuver set. SP is expected to lead the power with the G application so that the airspeed is held rather than recovered.

error_modes.label: EXIT HEADING CONTROL AFTER HIGH-G MANEUVERING

texts.0: SP, due to a rollout initiated without reference to the heading indication after the strain, did not exit the maneuver on the planned heading and did not recognize the error after the recovery. The exit heading was more than 10 degrees from the briefed value and no correction was initiated. The IP took the controls to re-establish the required heading before the next maneuver could be set up.
texts.1: SP, due to a rollout lead point that was not adjusted for the bank and G being flown, exited the maneuver 10 degrees from the planned heading. SP corrected the heading only after the IP called it verbally, and the delay meant the next entry was set up late. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout started slightly late on the first repetitions, exited the maneuver between 5 and 10 degrees from the planned heading. SP recognized the error immediately, corrected it with a smooth and coordinated input and adjusted the lead point on the following repetitions with no prompting or intervention from the IP.
texts.3: SP exited each high-G maneuver within 5 degrees of the planned heading, leading the rollout appropriately for the bank and G being flown and keeping the heading reference in the cross-check through the recovery. Corrections were coordinated, timely and made without prompting.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the planned heading with negligible error on every repetition, adjusting the lead point to the actual bank, G and rate of turn of each maneuver. The exits were coordinated and the aircraft was stabilized on heading immediately, with no secondary corrections required.
texts.marginal: SP exited the maneuvers within the required heading tolerance, but the error was consistently in the direction of an overshoot and was removed with a secondary correction after the rollout. The values stayed inside standards, yet the trend was toward a rollout lead point that was habitually too late. SP is expected to set the lead point from the actual turn rate so that the exit heading is achieved on the primary rollout.

error_modes.label: BREATHING CYCLE INTERVAL AND MAXIMUM STRAIN HOLD DURING AGSM

texts.0: SP, due to holding the anti-G strain for more than 3 seconds without breathing, did not keep the prescribed breathing cycle of approximately every 2 to 3 seconds during sustained loading above 3G. The prolonged breath hold reduced G tolerance and SP reported greying of the peripheral vision while still pulling. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and terminate the sequence, and the recovery produced deviations beyond 300 feet in altitude and beyond 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a breath hold that repeatedly exceeded 3 seconds, stretched the breathing cycle well past the prescribed 2 to 3 second interval and lost strain effectiveness toward the end of each loaded turn. SP restored the correct cycle only after the IP called the breathing verbally, and the correction came after several further seconds of loading. Altitude reached 300 feet from the assigned value and airspeed reached 20 knots from the target before the parameters were re-established, with no intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially long breath hold at the first G application, exceeded the 3 second limit on the entry to the first repetition. SP felt the loss of strain effectiveness, resumed the 2 to 3 second breathing cycle without any prompting and flew the remaining repetitions on the prescribed interval. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP kept the anti-G strain continuous while breathing approximately every 2 to 3 seconds and never held the strain longer than 3 seconds without breathing. The breathing cycle remained regular through every loaded turn, and altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP maintained a rhythmic strain and breathing cycle at the prescribed 2 to 3 second interval from the first G application to the unload, with no breath hold approaching the 3 second limit even at the highest G of the sequence. Aircraft control was unaffected by the breathing effort and deviations in altitude and airspeed remained negligible throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the strain and breathing cycle inside the prescribed interval, but the breathing was consistently at the far end of the 2 to 3 second window and lengthened further on the last repetitions of each set. No loss of vision or strain effectiveness appeared and the parameters stayed within standards, yet the trend was toward the 3 second breath hold that reduces G tolerance. SP is expected to shorten the breathing cycle so that a margin remains at the end of the maneuver set.

error_modes.label: STRAIN INTENSITY SCALED TO THE APPLIED G (AGSM CONTINUUM)

texts.0: SP, due to applying a fixed level of strain instead of treating the AGSM as a continuum, did not increase the intensity of the muscle contraction as the G increased through the loaded portion of the maneuver. The strain that was adequate at 2G was left unchanged at the peak of the turn and SP showed loss of peripheral vision and a delayed response to IP calls. The IP intervened on the controls to unload the aircraft, and the excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a strain intensity that was not matched to the applied G, kept the leg, abdominal and chest contraction at a low level while the G was still increasing and tightened it only late in the turn. SP raised the intensity after the IP called it verbally, and by then the aircraft had reached 300 feet from the assigned altitude and 10 degrees from the target exit heading. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a strain intensity set for the entry G rather than increased with the loading, entered the higher G portion of the first repetition undertightened. SP recognized the first symptoms, increased the contraction of the legs, abdomen and chest without prompting and flew the remaining repetitions with the intensity matched to the G. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 5 and 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.3: SP treated the AGSM as a continuum and increased the intensity of the strain as the G increased, while keeping all elements of the full manoeuvre present at the lower G levels as well. No symptoms appeared at any point of the sequence and altitude was held within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP modulated the contraction of the legs, abdomen and chest continuously with the applied G, using every element of the AGSM at the lower G levels at reduced effort and full effort at the peak of each turn. The scan and the control inputs were unaffected by the straining, and deviations in altitude, airspeed and exit heading were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP increased the strain intensity with the G and remained within standards, but at the lower G levels of the sequence some elements of the full AGSM were dropped rather than simply applied at a lower level of intensity. No symptoms developed and the parameters were met, yet the trend was toward an abbreviated manoeuvre whenever the G was moderate. SP is expected to keep every element of the AGSM present at low G and to vary only the level of effort.

error_modes.label: SUSTAINMENT OF THE STRAIN THROUGHOUT THE PERIOD OF INCREASED G-LOADING

texts.0: SP, due to relaxing the strain before the G loading was removed, did not maintain the AGSM throughout the loaded portion and released the muscle contraction while the aircraft was still above 3G. Symptoms appeared in the last part of the turn and SP did not respond to the first IP call. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft, and the resulting excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an early release of the strain, stopped the muscle contraction as soon as the target G was reached instead of maintaining it throughout the period of increased G-loading. SP reapplied the strain only after the IP called it verbally, and the delay allowed the deviation to reach 300 feet in altitude and 10 degrees on the exit heading before the parameters were re-established, with no intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a strain that faded in the second half of the first loaded turn, did not maintain the contraction for the whole period of increased G-loading. SP felt the effectiveness dropping, restored full tension without any prompting and held it to the unload on the remaining repetitions. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 5 and 10 degrees on the exit heading.
texts.3: SP maintained the strain at full muscle contraction from before the G onset until the loading was removed, with constant breathing cycles for the whole period of increased G-loading. No degradation of vision or aircraft control appeared and altitude was held within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP sustained the AGSM with unbroken muscle contraction and constant breathing cycles across every repetition, releasing the strain only after the aircraft was unloaded. The strain effort was carried without any effect on the scan or on the smoothness of the control inputs, and deviations in altitude, airspeed and exit heading were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the strain through the loaded portion and stayed within standards, but the contraction was noticeably tapering in the final seconds of each turn and was released a moment before the aircraft was fully unloaded. No symptoms appeared, yet the trend was toward an early end of the strain while G was still applied. SP is expected to hold the full contraction until the G loading is actually removed.

error_modes.label: RECOVERY ACTION AFTER GRAY OUT AT THE ONSET OF G FORCES

texts.0: SP, due to continuing to manoeuvre after gray out appeared at the onset of the G forces, did not return to 1 G flight and did not reapply the anti-G strain before continuing. Altitude and airspeed were not critical and an unload was available, but SP pressed on with the turn while the visual symptoms persisted. The IP had to take the controls, unload the aircraft to 1 G and terminate the maneuver, with deviations beyond 300 feet in altitude and beyond 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed decision after gray out at the G onset, kept the loading applied instead of returning to 1 G flight to reapply the strain. SP unloaded only after the IP directed it verbally and then re-entered the maneuver without re-evaluating the strain. Altitude reached 300 feet from the assigned value and airspeed reached 20 knots from the target during the recovery, with no intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a late recognition of the gray out at the onset of G, held the loading for a short period before returning to 1 G flight. SP then reapplied the anti-G strain, re-entered the maneuver smoothly and completed the remaining repetitions without symptoms, with no prompting or intervention from the IP. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP recognized the gray out at the onset of the G forces, returned to 1 G flight since altitude and airspeed were not critical, reapplied the anti-G strain and then continued manoeuvring. The re-entry was smooth and the remaining repetitions were flown without symptoms, with altitude held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP detected the first indication of gray out immediately, unloaded to 1 G with a smooth control input, re-evaluated and reapplied the strain, informed the IP and then re-entered the exercise. The whole sequence was flown without any degradation of aircraft control and the deviations in altitude and airspeed were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP applied the correct sequence after gray out, returning to 1 G, reapplying the strain and re-entering, but the unload and the re-entry were made with abrupt control inputs rather than smoothly. The parameters remained within standards and no further symptoms appeared, yet the trend was toward a hurried recovery that adds its own G transients. SP is expected to fly the return to 1 G and the re-entry smoothly.

error_modes.label: G-AWARENESS EXERCISE OR AGSM DEMONSTRATION BEFORE MANOEUVRES OF THREE OR MORE Gs

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the required pre-manoeuvre step, did not perform a G-awareness exercise or an AGSM demonstration before accomplishing manoeuvres that could require three or more Gs and entered the sequence directly. The effectiveness of the strain and the personal G-tolerance for the sortie were therefore never evaluated. The IP had to direct a knock-it-off and assume control to reset the profile, and the resulting excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to compressing the pre-manoeuvre flow, set up and entered the first maneuver that could require three or more Gs before performing the G-awareness exercise. SP accomplished the exercise only after the IP prompted verbally and the sequence had to be reset, with altitude reaching 300 feet from the assigned value and airspeed 20 knots from the target during the repositioning. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an out of sequence pre-manoeuvre flow, began the set-up for the aerobatic portion before accomplishing the G-awareness exercise. SP recognized the omission before applying more than 3G, unloaded, flew the exercise as described in Chapter 1 and then continued, with no prompting or intervention from the IP. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP accomplished a G-awareness exercise before any manoeuvre that could require three or more Gs, as described in Chapter 1, and confirmed both the effectiveness of the AGSM and the personal G-tolerance for the sortie. The exercise was flown in the assigned block with altitude held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP planned and accomplished the G-awareness exercise as an integral part of the pre-manoeuvre flow, briefed the intent, confirmed strain effectiveness and G-tolerance and moved into the high-G portion without any break in the profile. Altitude, airspeed and exit heading deviations during the exercise were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP accomplished the G-awareness exercise before the manoeuvres requiring three or more Gs, but it was flown immediately before the first aerobatic entry rather than early in the working area, leaving no room for a repetition if the strain had proved ineffective. The requirement was met and the parameters stayed within standards, yet the trend was toward treating the exercise as a formality at the entry. SP is expected to accomplish it early enough for the result to be usable.

error_modes.label: G-ONSET RATE DURING THE G-AWARENESS EXERCISE

texts.0: SP, due to a rapid rather than slow and smooth G-onset rate, reached the target G in a single abrupt pull and left no time to evaluate the effectiveness of the AGSM or to determine G-tolerance. The strain lagged the loading and SP showed visual symptoms at the peak of the pull. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft, and the excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an onset rate well above the slow and smooth rate required for the exercise, loaded the aircraft too quickly for the strain to be evaluated during the build-up. SP reduced the rate only after the IP called it verbally, and the abrupt entry drove altitude to 300 feet from the assigned value and airspeed to 20 knots from the target. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially quick pull at the entry to the exercise, applied a G-onset rate that did not allow the strain to be assessed as the loading built. SP recognized the abrupt entry, relaxed the rate to a slow and smooth build-up without any prompting and flew the following repetition correctly. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP applied a slow and smooth G-onset rate that gave sufficient time to evaluate the effectiveness of the AGSM and to determine G-tolerance before the target G was reached. The build-up was continuous with no steps in the pull, and altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP built the G at a uniformly slow and smooth rate, matching the strain to the loading at every stage and reporting the assessment of AGSM effectiveness and G-tolerance during the build-up. The entry produced no perceptible transient in pitch or bank, and deviations in altitude and airspeed were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP used a slow and smooth G-onset rate that met the requirement, but the build-up became progressively quicker on each successive repetition of the exercise. The rate remained usable for evaluating the strain and the parameters stayed within standards, yet the trend was toward an onset too rapid to assess AGSM effectiveness. SP is expected to keep the same deliberate rate on every repetition.

error_modes.label: ENTRY SET-UP OF THE G-AWARENESS EXERCISE (AIRSPEED, POWER, NOSE POSITION)

texts.0: SP, due to entering with airspeed well below the planning figure of approximately 200 to 220 KIAS and with power not set to maximum, did not establish a level or slightly descending turn capable of sustaining 4 Gs. The nose fell far outside 10 degrees of the horizon as SP tried to hold the G and the exercise could not be flown as described. The IP intervened on the controls to recover the attitude, and the excursion exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an entry airspeed below the 200 to 220 KIAS planning range with the power lever short of maximum, could not sustain the target G in a level or slightly descending turn. SP added power and adjusted the pitch only after the IP called it verbally, and by then the aircraft had reached 300 feet from the assigned altitude and 20 knots from the target airspeed. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried set-up, entered the exercise a few knots below the 200 to 220 KIAS planning range and with the power not yet at maximum. SP recognized the shortfall at the first G application, unloaded, reset maximum power and airspeed and re-entered with the nose within 10 degrees of the horizon, without prompting or intervention. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP set maximum power and entered the exercise with sufficient airspeed to sustain 4 Gs, flying a level to slightly descending turn with the nose kept within 10 degrees of the horizon. The set-up was completed before the G was applied, with altitude held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP established maximum power and an entry airspeed in the upper part of the planning range, then flew a level to slightly descending turn with the nose held close to the horizon and never beyond 10 degrees. The energy state supported the target G for the whole exercise and the deviations in altitude and airspeed were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP entered the exercise with maximum power and the nose within 10 degrees of the horizon, but the entry airspeed was at the bottom of the 200 to 220 KIAS planning range on every repetition, leaving no energy margin for the sustained turn. The exercise was completed within standards, yet the trend was toward an entry too slow to hold the target G to the end. SP is expected to set the entry airspeed with a margin above the planning minimum.

error_modes.label: TARGET G AND DURATION OF THE EXERCISE FOR FULL CARDIOVASCULAR RESPONSE

texts.0: SP, due to releasing the loading after a single breathing cycle, did not maintain approximately 4 Gs for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles, so the full cardiovascular response was never allowed and the AGSM could not be evaluated. SP then continued straight into the high-G portion of the profile on the basis of that incomplete exercise. The IP directed a knock-it-off and assumed control to reset the sequence, with deviations beyond 300 feet in altitude and beyond 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an AGSM cycle far shorter than the 10 to 15 seconds required, held the target G for only two breathing cycles and ended the exercise before a valid assessment could be made. SP repeated the exercise only after the IP prompted verbally, and the repositioning drove altitude to 300 feet from the assigned value and airspeed to 20 knots from the target. No intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an early unload on the first repetition, maintained approximately 4 Gs for fewer than the 4 to 5 breathing cycles required for full cardiovascular response. SP recognized the short duration, re-entered without any prompting and flew the second repetition for the full 10 to 15 second cycle. Deviations during the correction stayed between 150 and 300 feet in altitude and between 10 and 20 knots in airspeed.
texts.3: SP increased the loading to approximately 4 Gs and maintained it for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles, giving an AGSM cycle of 10 to 15 seconds and allowing the full cardiovascular response. The G level was held steady through the turn, with altitude within 150 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and exit heading within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP held approximately 4 Gs steadily for a full 10 to 15 second cycle with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles, reporting the assessment of the strain at the end of the exercise. The G level showed no fluctuation during the sustained turn and the deviations in altitude, airspeed and exit heading were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained approximately 4 Gs for the required duration, but every repetition was flown at the minimum of 4 breathing cycles and the last one was ended slightly earlier than the previous ones. The full cardiovascular response was still obtained and the parameters remained within standards, yet the trend was toward a cycle too short to evaluate the AGSM. SP is expected to plan the duration toward the upper end of the 10 to 15 second cycle.
